title: US-Iran tensions refuse to fade as fresh Strait of Hormuz attacks keep oil markets on edge
summary: While we haven't seen things escalate further recently, it is best to be reminded that US-Iran tensions are still very much simmering beneath the surface. And the IRGC is offering a reminder of that as they claim that four vessels were hit and caught fire in the northern Gulf, while three other vessels were reportedly struck by mines west of the Strait of Hormuz overnight. Besides that, Tehran is also warning that its response could extend to US bases across the region if Washington continues to encourage vessels to cross the Strait of Hormuz. The major concern here remains the fact that shipping through one of the world's most important energy routes remains vulnerable to further disruption. And even if oil supplies continue to flow, the threat alone is enough to keep shipping costs elevated and place a geopolitical premium into oil prices. So, that is hardly the kind of environment which will allow for oil markets to settle down comfortably. With that in mind, the situation also leaves broader market sentiment walking on eggshells. Sure, investors have not paid all too much attention to US-Iran developments as of late amid a lack of meaningful progress or escalation. However, the continued tensions and just the risk of things blowing up further could quickly bring oil prices, inflation worries, and risk aversion back into focus. title: European markets steady for now but widening bond yield spreads offer a warning
summary: European equities are keeping steadier so far today with France's benchmark CAC 40 index even holding up by 0.3% on the session. Meanwhile, the euro is also only slightly lower against the dollar but is still holding above the 1.1200 level at around 1.1215 currently. That suggests traders are not quite rushing for the exits just yet. That being said, I wouldn't be too quick to mistake the calmer mood for an improvement in the underlying risks for European markets. Not especially when the bond market is hinting at a different mood. The France-Germany 10-year yield spread has widened further to around 158 bps today, marking its highest level since 2011. And if you look at the chart, we're now revisiting levels last seen during the height of the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis. That's hardly a reassuring comparison, even if we are not quite talking about a repeat of those very same circumstances just yet. In any case, the widening spread reflects the growing premium investors are demanding to hold French debt over German bonds. And with France's fiscal troubles and political uncertainty showing little signs of easing, there isn't much reason for bond investors to feel more comfortable at this stage. So, what's next from here? It will be important to watch out for any concerns about how this story could develop into something that is not just France anymore. title: UK September CPI inflation rises to 3.5%, reinforces BOE November rate hike expectations
summary: UK September CPI +3.5% vs +3.4% y/y expected Prior +3.1% UK September core CPI +2.8% vs +2.8% y/y expected Prior +2.6% As expected, headline annual inflation surged in the Uk during the past month with the reading being the highest since October last year. Higher energy costs are the main culprit here as transport, particularly motor fuels, made the largest upward contribution to the change in annual price pressures. Of note, the average price of petrol rose by 8.2 pence per litre between August and September 2026, compared with a fall of 0.2 pence per litre between August and September 2025. The average price stood at 169.5 pence per litre in September 2026. This is the highest price recorded since August 2022. Besides the rise in headline prices, core prices also showed an uptick with the annual estimate climbing to 2.8%. This is one spot that will pressure the BOE to tighten policy further, reinforcing market expectations of a move in November next. Looking at the details, services inflation continues to run up to 3.7% in September from 3.4% previously. As such, that is a hint that price pressures are broadening and if not, it just reaffirms the notion that services inflation is still extremely sticky and stubborn. But whatever the case, it just means the BOE cannot rest on their laurels in trying to battle against the inflation monster. title: Heads up: UK September CPI inflation report due today, BOE rate hike for November almost fully priced in
summary: The UK CPI report for September is the main highlight on the economic calendar today, with the release due at 0600 GMT. The inflation numbers will be heavily watched as it will have a lot to say about what comes next on the BOE outlook, even if traders are almost fully pricing in another 25 bps move in November. Here's what to expect from the report: Headline CPI: +3.4% y/y expected (Prior +3.1%) Core CPI: +2.8% y/y expected (Prior +2.6%) The estimates show that another pickup in inflation pressures is expected this time around. That's hardly good news for the BOE with price pressures already running well above its 2% target. Higher energy costs are expected to remain a key driver, but I would argue that the more important thing to watch today will be the underlying inflation details. In particular, how stubborn services prices will be once again. Any signs of broader price pressures taking hold will only make the BOE's balancing act more difficult. Looking at market pricing, traders are already pricing in roughly 96% odds of a 25 bps rate hike for 5 November next. As such, I reckon even a hotter inflation reading will do little to change expectations for the immediate decision. Instead, it could strengthen the case for further tightening beyond November. title: Japan exports rise 16.7% for 13th straight month on AI chip demand, trade gap narrows
summary: The trade data is broadly supportive for the yen and for the BOJ’s tightening case, with exports still growing strongly and firms passing higher costs through to prices. The narrowing deficit owes much to oil disruption rather than weaker demand: Houthi rerouting delayed crude arrivals, so the import bill is likely to rebound in October as Suez-routed tankers arrive and procurement returns to around year-earlier levels. That makes oil prices and Middle East shipping the key swing factor for Japan’s trade balance and the yen’s import-driven pressure in the months ahead. For the BOJ , solid external demand adds to the case for a December hike, with its 30 October meeting and fresh forecasts the next focus. Japan’s exporters are still riding the AI boom, but September’s narrower trade gap owes more to delayed oil tankers than to any lasting improvement. For background. the US pending home sales report provides an early indication of demand in the existing housing market. Published monthly by the National Association of Realtors, it tracks signed contracts to purchase existing homes, rather than completed transactions. That distinction is what gives the report its value. A home typically goes under contract one or two months before the sale closes, making pending sales a leading indicator for the existing home sales report. It offers a more timely view of how buyers are responding to mortgage rates, prices and available inventory. The headline measure is the Pending Home Sales Index, with 100 representing the average level of contract activity in 2001. It is an index of activity, not a count of homes sold or a measure of prices. Markets generally focus on the monthly percentage change, alongside annual comparisons and regional details. Mortgage rates are a key driver. Lower borrowing costs can improve affordability and bring buyers back into the market, while higher rates can quickly reduce purchasing power. For background, the US housing starts report offers an early look at momentum in one of the economy’s most interest rate sensitive sectors. Published monthly by the Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development, it tracks construction of new privately owned homes, alongside building permits and housing completions. A housing start is recorded when excavation begins for a building’s foundation. The headline figure is reported at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, showing what a full year of construction would look like if that month’s adjusted pace continued. It is not the number of homes actually started during the month. For markets, the distinction between single-family and multifamily construction matters. Apartment projects can produce sharp swings in the headline, while single-family starts generally provide a clearer signal of underlying homebuilding demand. title: What are the main events for today?
summary: EUROPEAN SESSION In the European session, the main highlight was the UK employment report. The data beat expectations across the board and brought forward rate hike bets for the BoE. Tomorrow, we will get the UK CPI report which could strengthen expectations further in case the core figures come out hot. Looking ahead, we have the German ZEW survey which is expected to ease to 30.0 from 34.7 in the prior month. The data won't change anything for the ECB, though, so the market reaction will likely be muted. AMERICAN SESSION In the American session, we get the US housing starts and building permits data. The housing data hasn't been a market mover in this cycle, as the focus has been solely on AI which has been arguably the most important growth driver. Yesterday, we got the NAHB housing market index, which fell to the lowest level since 2012. The NAHB index generally leads the housing starts and building permits data, so we might get lower than expected figures today. All of this shouldn't be surprising amid elevated mortgage rates.
